title: Snoozer Hall's tone and Whiteman's St. Charles concert
summary: He describes Joe Capraro's guitar influences and Snoozer Hall's fiddle tone, then how he pressed Whiteman to play jazz at his concert.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I was wondering about Joe Coffero's style on guitar. Where did he get that?

That's, as far as I, I didn't know any, anybody. Well he did, some things he took off Snoozer. Yeah. Cause he and Snoozer were good friends. See when I had the band at the roof, Snoozer used to come up there and sit with us, whenever he was in town, you see. He'd come up there and sit there with us and play guitar and fiddle, you know. That scratchy fiddle. You ever hear him play fiddle? Never did. Oh man, you ain't heard nothing. You ain't like they say, you ain't heard nothing until you heard Snoozer play fiddle.
Was it good or is it funny?

It was marvelous Bill, but it was the stinkinest tone, it was like Fazola playing the saxophone. Fazola was the world's worst sounding saxophone player that you ever heard in your life. In fact, cause Benny Pollock, two or three times, well not only Pollock, but Miller. And a lot of the band wanted him to play the lead, cause Fazola was a marvelous musician, you know. I mean he read the seven clefs and all. But man, the tone he got out of the saxophone, the sound of Sidney Ironman, the same Rapolo was the same way. They sounded like fish horns, it didn't sound like a saxophone, you see. And well that's the kind of a tone that Snoozer got out of the fiddle. It didn't sound like a fiddle at all, but he played wonderful, you know, jazz, fine jazz. And there's a little story there. But I could tell you Snoozer used to come over and from Bogalus and sit in with us a lot of times. So Whiteman happens to be in town. They're playing the St. Charles Theater. And in the band is Bix, Trombauer, Izzy Freeman. That's the only, only jazz men in the band. So we all go to the concert. It was in two parts there, part and then, and the intermission and then another part. Well the whole first thing they never played one note of jazz, you see. So we're in the alley, Johnny Detroit could verify this. We're in the alley, we're talking to Whiteman, you see. So I was delegated to go talk to Whiteman about getting to play some jazz. Bix and Trombauer, especially because we didn't know Izzy Freeman so well then, you know. So I walked up and told him, I said, Paul, I said, we got to have some jazz. And I looked at me and Johnny, he and Johnny Detroit were talking and looking at me like that, you know. And I said, I mean, I said, we're going to have some jazz or else. See, so he says, well, I says, we don't have anything coming up. He says, the only thing we got, we're going to play things like Metropolis and American Empower. I said, well, it's a big band, a concert band, you see. So I told him, uh-uh, man, we got to have some jazz. So I looked at Johnny and he looked at me and Johnny says, well, the guys are, I said, man, there's 200 jazz men out there. They come in here to hear Bix and Trombauer, you see. So he says, well, I don't know. I said, well, I'll see what I can do, see. So they went back in, they got on and they started off with this American Empower. And they get about five minutes in and they cuts the band off like that. See, and he walks to the front of the stage and he says, ladies and gentlemen, says, I have a lot of, I've had a lot of requests and threats for Bix and Trombauer. And Roy Barger was playing piano. He says, for Bix and Trombauer. And he turns around and he looks at them and he says, boys, you're on your own. And he walks off the stage and they didn't know what to do, you know. They never had anything like that happen before, you know. So first thing you know, Roy Barger started swamping, singing the blues. So they played, they played singing the blues and they played Melancholy Baby and a couple of things that Trombauer played. And well then everybody was satisfied then. But they wouldn't have played one note of jazz in the whole concert if we hadn't done that, you know.
